doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

title: What makes the guitar unique: shifting note positions
summary: Juber explains how notes sit in several positions on the guitar and how musical knowledge combines with guitar-specific thinking.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Because you took classical, guitar has always mystified me a little bit. I’m a piano player and a saxophone player. But because you played classical and if you played an F major 7 and you’re looking at your hand, you know what the notes are.
But not all guitar players do I think.

True. Yeah I mean I’ve done concerts with guitar players who were purely primitive in their conception of the instrument but can do remarkable things. You don’t have to have the musical understanding. But what’s interesting about the guitar, and kind of unique I mean in the context of it being affordable, portable, versatile, and capable of making a complete musical statement because it incorporates rhythm, harmony, counterpoint, melody, all within its accessible performance, that what’s curious about the guitar is because the notes are not in fixed positions. You know you can change the tuning for example and the notes move. That if you understand music and you play guitar, then the meta information, the pure musical information, which never changes, I mean a C is always a C but it moves into different positions, depending on the context. Even a

standard tuning you could play a middle C in four, five different positions. The mental process there is different. Because on a piano a note is always a note. It doesn’t shift. And mostly on an orchestral instrument or a band instrument the notes are mostly in the same place. I mean you can do crazy fingerings and overblow notes and stuff on the sax, which is really cool, but on the guitar if you combine the musical education and the guitarology of it, the guitaristics of it, that’s where you get into some really interesting and unique musical areas. And that’s something that just completely engages me.
